items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: At that time, I was interested – I wanted to play like Del Staigers, who was a cornet soloist.

ctx.x: I was going to say, that’s interesting. At the age of whatever it was, 13, you were playing with Duke Ellington.

Yeah. In a sense, yeah. And they were always – they were very encouraging. All those fellows – Count Basie’s band, Erskine Hawkins and the Bama State Collegians – they would all – they would say, “Kid, you stick with it.” And they remembered me when I finally became a professional player. They’d say, “I remember you from that children’s program.” And Louis, he remembered me. He’d say, “I remember you when you was a little boy.” He was great. He came to – I came to Witham Theater, and they introduced me to him. So…
But you had a different idea of what music was at that age. About how old were you when you were doing all of this, when you were playing on the kids’ show?

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: But I remember Del Staigers for some reason or other better than the others, and I always wanted to play like Del Staigers

ctx.x: Were you aspiring to play in a classical situation at that time also?

Well yes I did, and even while I was with the band I always practiced a lot of classical things, not thinking that I would ever get an opportunity to play in a symphony orchestra, but I just did it because of my interest in that. And when I was younger I heard Del Staigers , who, he’s one, and I’m sure I heard Herbert Clarke and Walter Smith, people like that who were very famous cornet soloists. But I remember Del Staigers for some reason or other better than the others, and I always wanted to play like Del…

he did that. He brought them in. So I took it home and it was Del Staigers , and he had a very high pitched voice “and now when you do this —” you do so and so and so and so. He had a voice like that. But his playing was really beautiful. And of course the recording wasn’t that great because of the time at which it was done. So I thought to myself, now what can I do to put Dick Perry on when I go back with these recordings? And I had one of these big LP’s on rubber about that thick, those old recordings, it was…
